hook: The boy who worked in a factory at 12 and grew up to write Oliver Twist and A Christmas Carol.

pages.x: Charles Dickens was born in Portsmouth in 1812. When he was 12, his father was jailed for debt, and Charles was sent to work ten hours a day in a factory, pasting labels on pots of boot polish. He kept the shame a secret all his life.
pages.cap: The Marshalsea, the prison where his father was held

pages.x: He became a reporter, taking down speeches in Parliament in shorthand, and wrote funny sketches of London life under the name "Boz". In 1836 his comic Pickwick Papers made him the most famous writer in England at 24.

In Oliver Twist, the orphan in the workhouse dares to ask: "Please, sir, I want some more." His novels showed readers the cruelty of workhouses, child labour and debtors' prisons, and helped bring reform.
His novels came out in parts, a chapter or two each month. A famous story says that in 1841 crowds on the docks of New York shouted to sailors arriving from England: "Is Little Nell dead?"

In 1843 he wrote A Christmas Carol in six weeks. The miser Scrooge, who says "Bah! Humbug!" to Christmas, is visited by three ghosts and learns to be kind. It helped shape how Christmas is celebrated today.
He gave readings of his books to huge crowds in Britain and America, acting out every character with different voices. Audiences laughed, wept and fainted. The tours made him rich, but wore him out.

In 1865 his train fell off a bridge at Staplehurst. Dickens helped the injured and the dying, then climbed back into his dangling carriage to rescue the manuscript of his new novel. He died five years later to the day.
He died at his country home in 1870, aged 58, halfway through The Mystery of Edwin Drood, so no one will ever know who did it. He was buried in Westminster Abbey.
Dickens created some of the best loved characters in literature, from Scrooge to Oliver Twist, and his stories pushed Britain to care for its poor.
pts: Wrote Oliver Twist, A Christmas Carol and Great Expectations
Exposed the suffering of poor children
Helped shape the way we celebrate Christmas
